tldr: We propose FLORA, an open model suite for robotics data engines. It simultaneously generates timestamped action captions, process rewards, and outcome rewards needed for training robotics foundation models—matching frontier commercial VLMs while cutting inference costs by roughly $\sim 125\times$.
hero_caption: Overview of FLORA's core capabilities. It covers temporal segmentation and contextual action captioning (top), as well as outcome rewards for episode success, process rewards for step-level evaluation, and rubric-based grading (bottom)—all within a unified open foundation.
overview:
The biggest bottleneck in scaling robotics foundation models is the lack of high-quality annotation data. Correlating language instructions with physical actions during pretraining requires timestamped captions that pinpoint when and what happened. Post-training with reinforcement learning (RL) requires process rewards to evaluate progress at every step. Furthermore, real-world deployment monitoring and automated evaluation demand episode-level outcome rewards.

Labeling all of this manually is impossible. Relying on APIs from massive commercial vision-language models (VLMs) like GPT-6 Astra becomes prohibitively expensive across tens of thousands of video hours. Meanwhile, most existing open tools specialize in either captioning or reward modeling, but not both.

To bridge this gap, a team led by NVIDIA developed and open-sourced FLORA, an industrial-quality data engine built to train the GR00T robotics models. Based on the Qwen3.5 series, FLORA integrates temporal segmentation, contextual captioning, and multi-granularity reward prediction. It is battle-tested at scale, capable of processing 200,000 hours of video per day across a cluster of 512 GB300 GPUs.

Across multiple benchmarks, FLORA substantially outperforms existing specialized models and performs competitively with frontier commercial models like GPT-6 Astra. Crucially, it slashes inference costs by roughly $\sim 125\times$. This practical breakthrough enables researchers to run large-scale physical data pipelines locally.
contributions: Built FLORA, an open model suite that integrates temporal segmentation, contextual captioning, and outcome/process/rubric reward evaluation for robotics videos.
Introduced new benchmarks—DenseCaptionBench (300 episodes) and DenseRewardBench—to systematically benchmark fine-grained annotation across multi-view, bi-manual, and dexterous hand manipulation.
Optimized temporal boundary localization and descriptive accuracy using reinforcement learning (GRPO), matching or outperforming GPT-6 Astra in captioning and failure detection.
Demonstrated industrial-scale throughput by processing 200,000 hours of data per day at roughly $\sim 125\times$ lower cost compared to commercial APIs like GPT-6 Astra.

sections.heading: Open-sourcing the data engine at the heart of robotics learning
sections.summary: Every stage of the robotics foundation model life-cycle requires three types of labels: pretraining captions, RL process rewards, and evaluation outcome rewards. FLORA was built as an industrial-grade data engine that generates all three with high precision and low cost.
sections.details:
Robotics AI is rapidly shifting from single-platform policies to generalist models trained on diverse, heterogeneous, large-scale datasets. Training these models effectively relies not just on data volume, but on high-quality labels.

Required labels vary across training phases. The pretraining phase demands timestamped captions detailing action start/end times and descriptions to condition policies on language instructions. Next, the RL post-training phase requires process rewards to track step-level progress within an episode—similar to monitoring step-level reasoning in language models. Finally, real-world deployment and evaluation demand episode-level outcome rewards to judge whether an entire task succeeded.

However, no existing open system covers all of these needs, and relying on frontier commercial models becomes cost-prohibitive as datasets scale. FLORA resolves this challenge. Composed of three models—segmentation, captioning, and reward prediction—it is actively used to train GR00T models, proving its high throughput by labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300 GPUs.

captions.F1: Core tasks covered by FLORA: temporal video action segmentation (01), context-aware action captioning (02), episode-level outcome rewards (03), fine-grained process rewards including failure detection (04), and flexible grading against user-defined rubrics (05).

sections.heading: Matching frontier commercial models at 1/125th the cost
sections.summary: We evaluated FLORA on public and custom benchmarks. It rivals GPT-6 Astra across both captioning and reward tasks while outperforming specialized models, all while cutting inference costs by roughly $\sim 125\times$.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Timestamped Action Captioning
We evaluated both temporal segmentation and caption generation. On the public benchmark WGO-Bench (100 episodes), FLORA achieved a temporal segmentation F1 score of 50.3%, outperforming existing pipelines such as Refiner (33.4%) by 16.9 points. On Joint F1, which evaluates whether both temporal boundaries and captions match the ground truth, FLORA reached 34.5%, ranking second only to GPT-6 Astra (39.0%).
To move beyond single-view, parallel-jaw gripper setups, we introduced DenseCaptionBench (300 multi-view episodes), featuring 100 human manipulation, 100 parallel-jaw gripper, and 100 dexterous multi-finger hand videos. On human tasks (Human100), FLORA achieved the highest Joint F1 score of 37.4%, beating GPT-6 Astra (29.7%) by 7.7 points. On robot tasks (Robot200), FLORA scored 51.0% Joint F1, closely trailing Astra (57.9%).

### 2.2 Reward Labeling
On RoboRewardBench for outcome rewards, FLORA achieved an MAE (scaled by 100) of 40.0 against 1–5 ground-truth ratings. This represents a 27.8% error reduction over GPT-6 Astra (55.4) and the specialized RoboReward baseline (66.5). FLORA is especially strong at properly assessing partial successes.
On DenseRewardBench (4,861 steps), which assesses step-level progress, FLORA achieved a macro F1 of 46.2%. Its standout capability is failure detection: while baselines detected at most 11.7% of failure steps, FLORA achieved a 53.3% recall. On RubricBench, which scores against custom user criteria, FLORA achieved an L1 distance of 6.5 to human consensus, outperforming 9 out of 10 frontier generalist models.

### 2.3 Annotation Efficiency and Cost
Based on a 50-episode test on DenseCaptionBench, running FLORA on an 8x GB300 setup ($10/GPU-hour) costs approximately $0.72 per hour of raw video. In contrast, GPT-6 Astra API at its best inference settings costs $88.49 per hour. FLORA delivers comparable or superior quality at roughly $\sim 125\times$ lower cost.

sections.heading: Sharp observations that catch subtle physical failures
sections.summary: Qualitative analysis shows that FLORA captures fine-grained sub-actions at high density and accurately flags dropped objects or grasp slips as failures where GPT-6 Astra often misses them.
sections.details:
Comparing FLORA's outputs with GPT-6 Astra on real manipulation videos highlights FLORA's keen eye for detail.

In terms of temporal coverage, while Astra detected only 4 coarse segments across an entire episode, FLORA accurately captured 34 out of 37 reference segments (achieving an F1@0.5 of 82.9% versus Astra's 18.2%). During a wire insertion task where Astra mistook the components for flower petals, FLORA accurately disambiguated the roles of both hands: holding the connector with the left hand while inserting the wire with the right hand.

Decisive differences also emerge in reward evaluation. In a toy assembly scene where a part was dropped, Astra noted the dropped part in its reasoning text but still rated the step as "Suboptimal." In contrast, Flora-Rewarder correctly classified it as a "Failure," recognizing that task continuation was blocked. In another scene where a bottle was knocked over but did not fall off the table, Astra gave a complete failure score (1/5), whereas FLORA correctly assigned a partial progress score of 3/5, matching human ground truth.

captions.F5: Qualitative comparison between FLORA and GPT-6 Astra. FLORA demonstrates superior precision in dense boundary detection (top), bimanual role captioning (middle), and failure detection as well as partial success scoring (bottom).

sections.heading: A three-model architecture sharpened with reinforcement learning
sections.summary: FLORA consists of three models: temporal segmentation, contextual captioning, and reward prediction. Built on open Qwen3.5 models and trained using SFT and GRPO, they achieve high temporal precision and objective evaluation capabilities.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Timestamped Captioning Pipeline
To generate dense captions from long videos, FLORA uses a two-stage divide-and-conquer pipeline. First, the segmentation model processes a sliding window with surrounding context. It outputs relative timestamps for events starting and ending within the core region, along with continuation flags for events extending beyond the window. These window-level predictions are deterministically stitched together based on temporal overlap and continuation flags to reconstruct full episode timestamps.
Next, the captioning model generates instruction-style descriptions for each extracted segment. Crucially, the model receives not only target segment frames, but also non-overlapping context frames immediately preceding and following the segment (Before/Target/After). Providing this before-and-after context ensures accurate object identification and disambiguates user intent—even during failed attempts. Multi-view camera feeds are composited into a single mosaic image per timestamp.

### 4.2 Flora-Rewarder
The reward model uses a single unified model weight (based on Qwen3.5-27B) and switches between outcome rewards, process rewards, and rubric evaluations via prompt conditioning. For outcome rewards, it computes an expected value from token probabilities over discrete ratings (1–5) and normalizes it to $[0, 1]$. For process rewards, it assigns a 3-way label (Normal, Suboptimal, Failure) along with an explanation every 0.5 seconds. It slides a 16-second window by 10-second strides, using retrospective labeling where future frames inform past steps before stitching. For rubric evaluation, it uses a thinking mode to reason about step-level criteria and aggregates assigned scores.

### 4.3 Training Strategy: SFT and GRPO
The segmentation model is based on Qwen3.5-9B, while captioning and reward models build on Qwen3.5-27B. All models first undergo supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large human-annotated datasets.
To maximize annotation quality, we apply reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). For the segmentation model, LoRA parameters are optimized using verifiable rewards computed from boundary accuracy and tIoU-based F1 against ground-truth intervals. For the captioning model, a point-based quality reward credits essential elements (action, object, hand roles) and penalizes factual hallucinations. This results in precise descriptions with minimal hallucinations.

sections.heading: Toward large-scale automated data generation for robotics
sections.summary: FLORA is an industrial-quality data engine for training robotics foundation models, rivaling frontier commercial VLMs across major benchmarks. Open-sourcing the suite enables the community to scale custom datasets and accelerate human-to-robot transfer.
sections.details:
FLORA reliably produces every key annotation type required across the robotics foundation model lifecycle: timestamped captions, process rewards, and outcome rewards. Its direct role in training NVIDIA's GR00T models proves its production readiness beyond academic prototypes.

FLORA rivals premier commercial models like GPT-6 Astra while decisively outperforming existing specialized models. Moreover, running FLORA on local clusters costs roughly $\sim 125\times$ less than commercial APIs. This makes high-precision labeling across tens or hundreds of thousands of raw video hours computationally and financially viable.

By open-sourcing FLORA, the authors hope to empower research groups to scale their custom robotics datasets and unlock emerging frontiers such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer from human video demonstrations.

sections.heading: Behind the scenes: Multi-view mosaics and qualitative evaluations
sections.summary: The appendix details DenseCaptionBench criteria, multi-view mosaic formatting, mathematical formulations of GRPO rewards, and in-depth qualitative failure/success analyses.
sections.details:
The appendix compiles essential engineering insights behind FLORA's design and benchmarking.

### Multi-View Mosaic and Input Formatting
Synchronizing wrist cameras with third-person views is vital for manipulation. FLORA composites 3 to 4 camera streams into a single mosaic image per timestamp. For instance, 3 views are tiled horizontally to $1152 \times 288$ pixels, while 4 views are arranged in a $2 \times 2$ grid at $768 \times 576$ pixels, preventing visual token overflow. The internal frame rate is adjusted so Qwen3.5 timestamp tokens map directly to absolute video seconds.

### Strengths and Trade-offs Revealed by Qualitative Analysis
Detailed qualitative analyses (Figures 10 and 11) highlight clear behavioral trade-offs. On the positive side, FLORA captures high-density micro-actions and sensitively identifies physical interaction breakdowns, such as tool slippage or dropped parts, as failures. On the flip side, it tends toward over-segmentation—splitting what a human would consider a single unified action (e.g., wiping a plate) into excessive sub-segments—and occasionally confuses visually similar phases like placing versus reaching. Furthermore, tuning the model for high failure sensitivity results in a trade-off where roughly 11% of normal actions are misclassified as failures.

captions.F11: Detailed comparison between Flora-Rewarder and GPT-6 Astra. While Astra defaults to "Suboptimal" on dropped parts (c) and grasp slips (d), FLORA correctly identifies them as "Failures." It also assigns balanced intermediate scores to partial progress (e).

takeaways: A unified robotics data engine architecture covering contextual captioning, process rewards, and outcome rewards is essential for foundation model workflows.
Rather than simply prompting off-the-shelf VLMs, applying reinforcement learning (GRPO) to optimize temporal boundaries and factuality directly improves physical action annotations.
Compositing multi-view feeds into mosaics and conditioning caption generation on surrounding context frames (Before/After) significantly mitigates intent and object hallucinations.
Open 27B- and 9B-class VLMs, when specialized and optimized, can rival top commercial APIs while delivering over $100\times$ better cost efficiency.
limitations: High sensitivity to failure steps introduces a false positive tendency, misclassifying approximately 11% of normal manipulation steps as failures.
Temporal segmentation is prone to over-segmentation, frequently splitting coarse, unified manipulation tasks into overly fragmented sub-actions.
Because process rewards rely on retrospective labeling using future context frames, the current pipeline cannot be directly deployed for real-time online robot control.
